title_original: Using the Graphics of GTA, Sara Sadik Explores the Challenges France’s Muslim Youth Face
excerpt_original: Sadik’s video game-inspired films center the issues young, Muslim men and teenagers face in France, from employment to notions of masculinity.

blocks.text: Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot , a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet. The column will appear every other Monday.

“They say love comes at you when you least expect it. I swear, I’d almost given up. But I actually fell madly in love, again,” says Zine, the protagonist of Sara Sadik’s video game-inspired film Khtobtogone (2021). In the scene, he watches the sun set over the water, wearing an Adidas tracksuit and a Gucci crossbody bag. We follow Zine as he leaps from cliffs into the water with his friends, their 3D-rendered bodies twisting in the wind; takes his girlfriend on motorcycle rides along the coast; and delivers food to nowhere, all while wrestling with conflicting loyalties and emotions.

How can he become the man he wants to be for the woman he loves? And how can he reconcile that desire with the sacrifice and devotion he feels he owes his friends, who have protected him and one another in a hostile world?

I first saw Khtobtogone at Sadik’s solo show “Seul sous la capuche” at THIRD BORN in Mexico City, and was struck by how a work made with the somewhat clunky graphics of Grand Theft Auto could be so moving. The piece has since appeared in several group exhibitions, including “Beyond the Manosphere: Masculinities Today” at Kunstmuseum St. Gallen, where it remains on view through January 2027, and “Harder Better Faster Stronger – Are Men OK?” at Fotografiska in Stockholm, on view through February 2027.

Sadik’s films, which are often made using video games, 3D software, or 360 cameras that mimic video game camerawork, take as their main subject the intimate life of young, French, muslim men and teenagers. They are often set in masculinized spaces, like shisha lounges, and deal with different facets of their lives, whether it’s grief, as in Crystal Zastruga (2023), the gamification of labor, as in TALS&TALOS MARKETPLACE (2026) (on view at Le Large , Île Seguin until March 2027), or, masculine hierarchies as in Ultimate Vatos: Force and Honor (2022) (which was recently screened at the “ 3HD Festival ” in Berlin).

blocks.caption: An installation view of “Seul sous la capuche” at THIRD BORN in Mexico City, Mexico. Courtesy THIRD BORN

blocks.text: Born in Bordeaux, she received her training at the École supérieure des Beaux-Arts de Bordeaux before moving to Marseille where the majority of her body of work is set. When we spoke by phone, she discussed how she develops her films through workshops with local communities in Marseille, the Paris protests, and why the positive reception of Khtobtogone irritated her. The following conversation has been edited for clarity. Shanti Escalante-De Mattei: How did masculinity become a central theme in your work? When I graduated, I moved to Marseille. There, I held a workshop with a group of teenagers, with the idea that I would produce something out of the encounter. But for me, the most important thing was to really connect with them and establish some kind of relationship. So we spent a lot of time simply talking and hanging out. The boys in the group began telling me about their problems. Because I was an outsider, they felt very comfortable sharing these stories with me and asking for advice. What kind of problems were they coming to you with? I would say the most talked about subject is love, like romantic love. They always ask for advice about this. Other than that, issues related to mental health: depression, and the sadness they experience in their daily life. These aren’t topics that they bring up much with their parents or even their friends. After this workshop, I was like, okay, maybe this is something I can work with. And they reminded me so much of my little brother. How so? Well, I haven’t represented my little brother directly in my work, but he’s there unconsciously, in some way. Obviously, it’s important to me to represent black and brown men from less privileged backgrounds because I come from this culture. My father is Moroccan, my mom is Algerian, I was born and raised in France, and I come from a working-class background. The stories [of this community] are not represented. Every time I have a new commission, the first thing that comes to my mind is who I want to work with. I choose where I’m going to do the workshop; it could be a school, a social center, or not jail, but [a juvenile detention center]. Or I focus on just one person. And that was the case with Khtobtogone [(2021)], as I understood it. Could you tell me more about how this work came together? Around the time that I received the commission [from the Centre National Des Arts Plastiques] Ahmed [Ra’ad Al Hamid] followed me on Instagram. He had thought I was someone else but then we started talking. He’s much younger than me, and we became friends, but with a big-sister, little-brother dynamic. And so obviously, romantic love came up. He was in love and would ask me for advice. At some point, I told him I wanted to make a film based on his story. He started sending me voice notes about his love story, but also just about his daily life.

The film is made using Grand Theft Auto V and was your first to use a video game engine. Why did you decide to tell this story through the format of a video game? At the time, there was a trend on YouTube of people creating French rap music video clips using GTA 5. They created wrappers [software that interacts with the video game to introduce visual elements, such as clothing and characters] to recreate the music videos using the game’s cinema mode. I worked with Diego [Grandry, mods creator and image director] to create the characters, clothes, and accessories specific to French culture. The protagonist of Khtobtogone works as a food delivery driver. There’s been a lot written about the gamification of gig work organized through apps. Was that something you wanted to explore in the film?

At the time, it was a side story in the film. It was only afterward that people started talking more about the conditions of delivery workers, how they are treated like slaves, and the impact these platforms have on mental health. Actually, it’s funny: my little brother just started doing this work. I really focused on these themes in TALOS&TALS MARKETPLACE [from 2026]. It’s about two friends attend a who vocational school [to train as] autobody mechanics. They are 17 and talk about the struggle to find a job, because of discrimination mainly. I wanted to explore this through the gamification of job-finding platforms. Even the state [employment] platform, France Travail, uses gaming tools like VR [virtual reality]. Through this, you can spend like a day in this job, to ‘discover’ it. They also develop these job simulator games for all these candidates in vocational schools to play. All teenagers [attending] these types of schools and looking for a job connect to this platform, which is like a video game, and they wait for a recruiter to hire them. This is how a teenager has to spend the entire day, from eight in the morning to six in the [evening], waiting for someone to hire them. And the recruiter can compare different profiles, analyze [candidates], like on Tinder. They even have this “wish list.” They’re treated like products.
How do you feel about video game aesthetics and narrative systems, which you enjoy so much, being appropriated in this way?

It angers me, because it’s not just in [the labor market]. France also uses video games to recruit teenagers to join the army. Every year, they run a campaign using Call of Duty , saying things like, “It’s better than playing on your computer, it’s the same, but in real life.” I made Ultimate Vatos [ :Force and Honor (2022)] about this. Right, and this work really focuses on themes of loyalty and obedience in masculine spaces, not just within the army but also the communities that marginalized men build together. Could you tell me a little more about how this work came about? Ultimate Vatos came after Khtobtogone , which a lot of people loved. The character in that film is super vulnerable. There was something in the reception of that film that bothered me. It was like, okay, I’m happy that you like seeing this guy being super vulnerable and sad, wanting to die. These teenagers and young men I work with, yes, they are vulnerable and have love stories, but they also have real fucking problems. What kind of emotions does society accept in Arabic men, in Black men? They’re vulnerable, but they’re also fighters. They are hungry; they find ways of resisting. So I wanted to make a film with another kind of emotion. And that brings me to the protests in Paris. There has been a great deal of Islamophobia in the coverage of and response to them. What has your reaction been? I’ve been out of France since the youth movement started, so I’ve been spending all my time on TikTok trying to figure out what is happening. The first couple of weeks, I really loved what I was seeing. Teenagers were making videos documenting their movements with their own references, which obviously comes from popular culture like anime and manga and video games, but also from historical figures. I found it really beautiful and super representative of why I like working with them. They have so much to say. Not a lot of people want to hear them; they think they’re dumb, but for me Gen Z is the best generation. But then obviously the first protests arrive with the police violence and the French media being racist and Islamophobic 24/7. Then there was this racist attack where a man was killed, and several people were injured. A child was injured and is still in the hospital. So, it became a nightmare. What has it been like seeing all of this through social media? It’s been awful to not be home during this. But I started making an archive of everything I was seeing for about a month now and I’m super glad I did because all these videos are being deleted on TikTok, Instagram, Twitter, especially videos documenting police violence. So, I have around 1,000 videos I’m protecting. Maybe in five years someone will need them for something. Having worked with teenagers for so long, especially in schools, did you see this coming at all or was it a surprise? I saw the conditions in the schools. They are really shitty, unsanitary. And there is so much discrimination in how students are chosen for university after they finish their baccalaureate. I didn’t think they would start this movement, but it doesn’t surprise me, they have a right to do this. I respect the complaints and I’m proud of them.
